content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

Happy to help you shape this. Before we get into anything concrete, I'd like to understand the *why* behind it, because that usually shapes what the app should actually do.

A few things I'm curious about:

1. **When this bookmarks app is finished and working well, what's different about your day compared to now?** For example — is the pain right now that you lose links you meant to read, that you can't find things you saved months ago, that they're scattered across different browsers and devices, or something else entirely?

2. **What's the moment you picture using it most?** The moment you're *saving* something, or the moment you're *coming back to find* something you saved earlier?

3. Right now, roughly **who is this for** — just you, or you imagine other people using it too?

You don't need to answer in any structured way — just tell me in your own words what's been bugging you that made you think "I should build this."

Honestly, it's a mix of things, but the biggest one is that I save links everywhere and then they just… disappear into a black hole. I'll come across an article I mean to read later, or a recipe, or some reference thing for a project, and I bookmark it — and then a month later I know I saved *something* about it but I can't find it. My browser bookmarks are a mess, and half of them are on my laptop and half on my phone.

So it's less "I lose links the second I save them" and more "I can never dig them back out again." When I do go looking, I'm trying to remember a word that was in the title, or roughly what it was about, and I just want to type that in and have it come up.

To your second question — it's really both moments, but if I had to pick, the *coming back to find it* moment is where the pain is worst. Saving needs to be quick and painless so I actually do it, but finding is where I'm currently suffering. And I'd also love to just… park things I intend to read but haven't gotten to yet, so they don't get lost in the pile.

For now this is just for me. I'm not thinking about other people using it — I just want to get my own stuff under control.

That's really clear, thank you — and it actually points to something important about what this app *is*.

Here's what I'm hearing, and I want to check I've got the direction right:

The core of this isn't really "a place to store bookmarks" — you already have plenty of those, and that's exactly the problem. The real goal is **being able to dig something back out later**, even when all you remember is a stray word from the title or a vague sense of what it was about. Saving matters, but only because it has to be effortless enough that you'll actually do it — the saving is a *means*, and the payoff is the *finding*.

So I'd summarize the goal as something like:

> "I want to stop losing track of things I've saved. When I vaguely remember saving something, I want to type in whatever I can recall and have it come back up — instead of it vanishing into a black hole across my laptop and phone. And I want a place to park things I mean to read but haven't gotten to yet, so they don't get buried."

Two things I want to confirm:

1. **Does that summary capture it** — is "finding things back" the heart of it, with saving as the thing that just needs to stay out of your way?

2. You mentioned laptop *and* phone, and things being scattered across both. Is **having it work across both of those** part of what "getting it under control" means to you — or would you be happy, at least to start, if this lived in one place and you just went there to save and search?

Yes — you've captured it really well. That summary is spot on. Finding things back is the heart of it, and saving just needs to stay out of my way so I actually keep doing it. Reading that back, it's exactly the itch I've been trying to scratch.

On the second question — I think I muddled that a bit. The scattering across laptop and phone is really just a *symptom* of the mess I'm in now, not a feature I'm asking for. What I actually want is one place where everything lives together, so it's not split up anymore. As long as it's one home for all of it that I can get to when I sit down to use it, I'd be perfectly happy to just go there to save and search. I'm not asking for anything clever syncing between devices — I just don't want my stuff living in five different places like it does today.

So: one tidy place, and getting back what I've saved. That's the win.

> Up near the search box there's a row: "Round up: recipe / work / reference / read later." Click **recipe**. Click it again to release.
> *(You gather from a fixed row of all your labels at the top, without hunting for a card first.)*

> In the same search box you already know, just **type `recipe`**. The recipes gather themselves, the same way searching does.
> *(One box for everything — labels are just more words the search understands.)*

As you go, the thing I'm listening for: **which one feels most like how you'd reach to gather a kind of thing** without having to stop and think? And a nudge to test the difference for real — in **A**, try gathering "work": you'll notice you first have to *find* a card that has the "work" label before you can click it. In **B** and **C** you don't. Does that matter to you, or not really?

Tell me which one clicks — and it's fine to say "this one, but borrow that bit from another."

I tried all three doing the recipe round-up, and then went back and gathered "work" like you suggested — and that test really did decide it for me.

**B is the one that clicks.** The row of labels sitting right up by the search box is exactly how I'd reach for it. I click "recipe" and there they are; click "work" and there those are — and crucially I never had to go *hunting* first. That matters more than I expected. In **A**, gathering "work" meant I had to scroll down and spot a card that happened to be tagged "work" before I could even click into it — and the whole reason I'm rounding things up is that I *can't* easily find them, so needing to find one first is a bit backwards. And there's another thing B quietly does that I love: it shows me *all* the labels I've got. I'm not going to remember every label I've ever made, so seeing them laid out ("recipe / work / reference / read later") is half the value — it reminds me what's even in there.

A couple of things to fold in, though.

Keep the nice bit from **A**: when I *am* looking at a card, being able to click the little label right on it to say "more like this" felt natural too. So — the row up top for when I'm gathering cold, and clickable labels on the cards for when I'm already looking at one. Both, ideally.

**C** made me a bit nervous, and here's why. Because the label is just typed as a word into the same box, I couldn't tell whether I was rounding up things I actually *filed* as "recipe" or just things that happen to *say* "recipe" somewhere. With my little pile it looked fine, but I can already picture it going wrong — imagine I have a label like "reading" and half my descriptions also use the word "read"; typing it would sweep in a load of stuff I never filed that way, and my tidy roundup gets muddied. When I gather a *kind*, I want *only* that kind — clean. I'd want the app to know the difference between "this is one of my labels" and "this is just a word I'm searching for."

One more, while we're here: once I've rounded up my recipes, I'd still like to be able to type a word to narrow *within* them — like recipes, then "pasta." That seemed to work in B, which is another point in its favour. And now and then I could see wanting two labels at once, but don't let me run ahead of you — B's the direction.

Here's the full picture of everything we've settled — the whole app, in plain terms, as one connected thing. You can open `prototypes/app.html` to see it all working together.

## What we've built

**① Finding — the heart of it**
Type whatever you half-remember and it comes up. It's forgiving on purpose: any words in any order, spaces and all; it looks inside the title, the description, your own note, *and* the site's readable name; it matches from the start of words (so "read" won't drag out "bread"); and it highlights *why* each result showed up. When nothing matches, it says so plainly.

**② Rounding up a kind**
Every item wears little labels. A quiet row of *all* your labels lets you gather a kind in one click (and reminds you what's even in there); you can also click a label on any card. Roundups are clean — they gather only what you actually *filed*, never things that merely mention the word — and you can narrow within a roundup by typing. There's always an obvious "show all again" way back.

**③ Saving — effortless, and yours**
Paste a link and the title, site and a description fill themselves in. You add your *own note* in your own words ("Sarah's birthday") — and that's searchable too. Labels nudge you toward ones you already have so you don't splinter into "recipe/recipes." Paste something twice and it won't make a duplicate — it takes you to the one you have. If it can't read a page, it still lets you save by naming it yourself; if it isn't a link, it kindly tells you why one's needed.

**④ Tidying — without fear**
Fix little things right on the card (note, labels); open "Edit details" for the bigger ones (title, description, even the link if a page moved). **Set aside** tucks things out of the way, reversibly; **Delete for good** is there for real rubbish — and **Undo** covers both, so no slip ever costs you anything.

**⑤ The quiet edges**
A welcoming day-one screen; an "everything's tucked away" reassurance instead of a scary blank; graceful behaviour when a page won't read; and a small, remembered **Order** control (newest / oldest / by name) that holds across searches and roundups.

## Deliberately set aside for later
- **Gathering by two labels at once** — you parked this; we'll come to it if you want it.
- **Site icons** next to each name, and staying **fast at large sizes** — noted as polish, not part of the core flows.

---

This is the scope I'd build for real. It's single-user, one home in your browser, no cross-device syncing — exactly as you framed it at the start.

**May I go ahead and start implementing this scope?** Nothing changes about what you've approved — this just moves us from exploring to building it properly.

Reading this all laid out — yes, I recognise my app in it. That's genuinely what I was hoping to end up with, and seeing finding, saving, rounding up and tidying described as one connected thing, it hangs together. Most of this is a clear "yes, build it."

But before you lock the scope, there's one thread I want to pull on, because it goes right back to the very first thing I told you. Remember I said the two halves of my pain were "I can never dig things back out" *and* "I want a place to park things I mean to read but haven't gotten to yet"? The digging-out half you've nailed. The reading half, though, I don't think is quite handled — it's quietly become just an ordinary label called "read later," and the more I sit with that, the more it worries me.

Here's the thing in my own experience. When I save an article I haven't read, I want to quickly flag "I still need to read this" — ideally right as I save it, without fishing for a label. Then I want to be able to glance at *just* the stuff I haven't read yet, in one spot, like a little to-do pile. And — this is the part a plain label doesn't do — once I've actually read something, I want to tick it off so it drops out of that pile on its own. With it being just a label, I'd have to remember to go back and peel the label off by hand every time, and I know myself: I won't. So that "to read" pile would slowly fill with things I've already read and things I never will, and it'd rot into exactly the untrustworthy heap I started with. That's the one corner where I can feel my original problem creeping back in.

So it's not a "label" in my head — it's more like a *state* a bookmark is in: unread, then read. Could we make "things to read" a proper little part of the app — a one-tap "haven't read this yet," a way to see only those, and an easy "mark as read" that clears it — rather than leaning on me to manage a label? That, to me, is core, not polish.

Everything else in your picture — please, go ahead and build it, I don't want to reopen any of it. The two-labels-at-once and the site icons I'm happy to leave parked as you've listed. It's really just: let's make sure the "stuff I mean to read" actually behaves like a reading pile before you call the scope closed. Sort that in, and you have my yes wholeheartedly.

That one I can live with as a follow-on.

Here's the fix, and it goes right at your hard condition.

**What changed:** your bookmarks now get a stable *home* to be kept in. Instead of double-clicking the file, you open the app with a **launcher** — double-click:

- **Mac:** `start.command`  ·  **Windows:** `start.bat`  ·  **Linux:** `start.sh`

A little window pops up and your browser opens the app. You open it the *same way every time* — no special incantation to remember, just "double-click the launcher." From that stable home, saving sticks properly. *(It uses Node, the same engine the app is built with; the README has the details.)*

**And a safety net, because you said the unforgivable thing is losing stuff you trusted:** if you ever open it in a way the browser won't save from, the app now shows a plain warning at the top — "this browser isn't letting me keep your bookmarks; use the launcher" — so it can *never* quietly forget and let you down.

**Please re-run your hard-condition journey:**
> 1. Double-click the launcher for your computer; the app opens in your browser.
> 2. Save a few things — the olive oil cake with a note, a couple more — do some edits, set one aside.
> 3. **Close the browser tab completely. Then open the launcher again** (or revisit `http://localhost:4321/`).
> 4. Everything you saved should be sitting right there — cake, note, edits and all — and searchable by your own words.

To be straight about what I did and didn't change:
- The persistence *logic* was always correct — I've now got an automated "save → close → reopen → still there" test proving it, plus a test that the warning shows when saving is blocked. The real fix is giving it that stable home so your browser keeps the data.
- One honest caveat: the launcher needs Node.js on your machine (free, one-time). If that's a problem for how you'll actually use this, tell me — there are other routes (a packaged app), they just reopen the "no install" question we'd settled.

**On auto-fill:** noted and agreed — you accept the graceful "type-the-title" fallback for now, and full "reads the page for you" for *all* sites is the **very next job**, not "someday." I'll line it up as the top of the next cycle the moment you accept.

But you've made it painless where it counts: a one-off free thing, and then it's just double-click-the-launcher every day, same as ever — no incantations. For keeping my stuff safe forever, that's a trade I'll happily take. No need to chase the packaged-app route on my account unless it ever becomes easy; the launcher's fine.

This is the thing I walked in wanting: one calm home for everything I save, that lets me dig things back out by whatever scrap I half-remember, keeps a proper pile of what I mean to read, lets me tidy without fear, and — now — actually remembers it all when I come back. Thank you for the patience with all my niggles along the way; it's landed somewhere I'm genuinely happy with.
